sections.overview: Mya arenaria is a burrowing marine bivalve native to the northwest Atlantic and now established on many European coasts and elsewhere after human transport.
sections.identification: Its thin, elongated oval shell remains gaping at both ends, and two long siphons reach the sediment surface while the animal stays buried.
sections.habitat: It buries itself in sand or mud on tidal shores, estuaries and lagoons, from the intertidal into shallow subtidal water, and tolerates a broad range of salinities.
sections.diet: Water drawn through its inhalant siphon supplies suspended food, especially phytoplankton and other organic particles, before leaving through the exhalant siphon.
sections.behavior: It lives mostly buried in a mucus-lined vertical burrow and extends its paired siphons through the sediment to feed and exchange water.
sections.reproduction: The sexes are separate and release gametes into the water for external fertilization; planktonic larvae later settle onto the seabed.
sections.ecology: As a suspension feeder it recycles planktonic production and is prey for fish, crabs and shorebirds; abundant introduced populations can compete with native bivalves.
sections.conservation: SeaLifeBase lists the global IUCN Red List category as Not Evaluated; this differs from the documented ecological effects of introduced populations in some regions.
